description: We are XmartAgro, from Uruguay. We chose Field Shift because drought hits our farmers hard: 2022/23 cost the country USD 1,883 million. Fernando Rivero, senior electronic engineer and software developer, leads hardware and architecture. Nicolas Eugui and Lisandro Gomez, young developers, built the engine and web app. Simon Rivero, 6, is learning to code with Scratch. We share a passion for space, our planet and solving complex challenges together.
summary:
XmartAgro is a web app that helps rainfed farmers in Uruguay decide what to plant, field by field, from a phone or a computer. It shows how much usable water is in the soil today and estimates soil health. It then replays 39 past seasons of NASA POWER weather (1987–2025) on that field. The result is simple: “in 7 out of 10 past seasons, this soybean had enough water.”

The farmer compares at least three crop or rotation options, including the current one. Each option explains why it fits, the evidence behind it, its expected benefits, what information is still missing, and its risks.

NASA SMAP soil moisture and MODIS NDVI feed a calibrated water-balance model. NDVI is also used to pre-fill each field’s crop history. Our edge is local data: low-cost soil sensors that correct the satellite, and the history and outcomes farmers confirm. A machine-learning layer learns from all fields and adjusts to each one.

The 2022/23 drought cost Uruguay USD 1,883 million. Run backwards, our model ranks that season as the worst of 39 for soybean. The tool turns complex satellite data into decisions farmers can use.
details:
What it does and how it works

XmartAgro is a web app for rainfed (secano) farmers. It runs in the browser of any phone or computer, with no app to download. For each field it answers three questions:

  1. How much water is in the soil today? A daily water-balance model uses NASA POWER rain and temperature. It is calibrated against NASA SMAP L4 root-zone soil moisture and estimates the usable water in the root zone, in mm.
  2. How risky is each crop option? We replay 39 real past seasons of NASA POWER weather (1987–2025), starting from today’s soil water. The app shows the result as 10 drops: “in 7 out of 10 past seasons, this soybean had enough water.” Blue means it had water, amber means it was tight, red means it ran out. This is not a forecast. It is the field’s real history of risk.
  3. How is the soil doing? MODIS NDVI (since 2000) detects which crop was grown each season and the bare-soil months. From that it proposes the field’s rotation history, and the farmer only confirms it and rates how each season went. The agronomist can add a soil test and the Soil Use Plan.

The farmer compares at least three crop or rotation options, including the current one. Each option explains why it fits, the evidence behind it, its expected benefits, what information is still missing, and its risks.

Local data is our edge. Optional low-cost soil sensors at 30 cm correct the satellite estimate for their field and for similar fields nearby. They measure every 3 hours and send once a day. The farmer’s confirmed history teaches the model what a bad season really means on each farm. A machine-learning layer learns from all fields and adjusts to each one: a new field starts from what its neighbors taught, and its own data weighs more every season.

Benefits and intended impact

The 2022/23 drought cost Uruguay USD 1,883 million (MGAP-OPYPA). Soybean fell to 707 kg/ha (INIA), and 28% of the summer crop area was not harvested (DIEA). Run backwards on NASA data, our model ranks 2022/23 as the worst of 39 seasons for soybean, which matches what farmers told us. XmartAgro helps farmers choose the crop, rotation and sowing date, and decide whether to buy insurance, knowing the real water risk of each field. It also makes soil health visible over time.

Tools used

  • NASA data: POWER (daily weather API), SMAP L4 and L3 (via AppEEARS), MODIS MOD13Q1 NDVI, GPM IMERG (rain check).
  • Modeling: a water-balance model calibrated by differential evolution; machine learning (regression and random forest / gradient boosting) for the learning layer.
  • Software: [Node.js / Python, the web framework and the database you actually used].
  • Hardware: low-cost soil moisture sensors with LoRa, NB-IoT or Wi-Fi. For the demo, sensor data is simulated and always labeled “Demo mode”.
  • [AI tools used to build the prototype, e.g. coding assistants, and what for.]

Creativity

  • The satellite pre-fills the history, so the farmer only taps to confirm.
  • Results are shown as “X out of 10 past seasons” instead of a forecast nobody can promise.
  • Each field’s own data gradually weighs more than the regional rule.
  • The engine is modular: a global NASA core plus a swappable local module (Uruguay today; SSURGO in the US, SoilGrids anywhere).

Factors we considered

  • Farmers: we surveyed 12 producers in Soriano, Río Negro and Paysandú, Uruguay (24,280 ha). 9 of 12 named drought as the cause of their last bad season, 12 of 12 would allow a sensor, and 11 of 12 have Wi-Fi.
  • Leases: many fields are leased for about 5 years, so the tool must be useful from the first season.
  • Starting from zero: base mode works with NASA data only, without sensors or history.
  • Honesty: there are no profit calculations and no “best crop”; the farmer and the agronomist decide. Generative AI never computes the numbers. Crop parameters are still provisional and will be sourced from FAO-56.
  • Cost and connectivity: sensors are optional, low-cost and only a few per 1,000 ha; the app keeps the last result if the signal drops.
